claim: Across all 655 overlapping 25-year windows starting each month from January 1947 (the last ending August 2026), a pension paying a fixed dollar amount lost at least 40.64% of its purchasing power; that best case is the window starting May 1995 (start code 199505), which spans the low-inflation years of the late 1990s and 2010s. The median 25-year loss was 57.87%, the worst 76.37%, and 70.99% of windows lost more than half. Over 30-year windows the smallest loss was 48.54% (median 71.85%). Even the calmest stretch of US inflation since the war left a no-raise pension buying about 40% less by its 25th year.

numbers.definition: Count of start months s from 1947-01 onward with s+300 months <= 2026-08 and CPIAUCNS present at both s and s+300 (CPIAUCNS = CPI-U all items, NSA, monthly; 2025-10 has no value, so the window starting 2000-10 is dropped).
Minimum over those windows of (1 - CPIAUCNS(s)/CPIAUCNS(s+300 months)) x 100: purchasing power lost by a fixed nominal payment after 25 years.
Start month s of the window with the minimum 25-year loss, written as year*100+month.
Median (statistics.median, mean of the two middle values if even count) of the 25-year losses x 100.
Share of 25-year windows whose loss exceeds 0.5, x 100.
Same as min_loss_25y_pct with 360-month windows (start 1947-01 to 1996-08, windows with a missing endpoint dropped).

assumptions: A fixed pension pays the same nominal amount every month with no cost-of-living adjustment; purchasing power is measured with CPI-U (all items, NSA).
Windows start every month and overlap; loss compares the price level in the first month of payment with the price level 25 (or 30) years later.
Missing CPI month (October 2025) is not interpolated; any window with that month as an endpoint is dropped.

series.provider: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis
